Instructed
in-STRUK-ted
v. (past part.)
From Latin instruere, to build into, to furnish, to equip — the same root as structure. Webster 1828: taught; educated; directed; informed. The Latin figure is architectural: to instruct a man is to build something into him.

Biblical Definition

Instructed in the Authorized Version is never mere information transfer; it is equipping. Our Lord uses it of the scribe who has been trained for the kingdom: every scribe which is instructed unto the kingdom of heaven is like unto a man that is an householder, which bringeth forth out of his treasure things new and old (Matthew 13:52) — a man with a stocked storehouse, holding both testaments and able to produce what the moment needs. Luke describes Apollos as one instructed in the way of the Lord who nevertheless knew only the baptism of John, and Aquila and Priscilla took him and expounded unto him the way of God more perfectly (Acts 18:25-26) — instruction can be genuine and still incomplete, and a mighty man in the scriptures received correction from a tentmaker and his wife. Paul’s own use is the most striking, because the schooling was in circumstances rather than in doctrine: I know both how to be abased, and I know how to abound: every where and in all things I am instructed both to be full and to be hungry, both to abound and to suffer need (Philippians 4:12). The verb there is the word for initiation into a mystery. Contentment is not a temperament; it is a thing learned, and hunger is one of the classrooms.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster 1828 defines INSTRUCT as to teach; to inform the mind; to educate; to direct or enjoin; and derives it from the Latin for building or furnishing. The architectural metaphor — building something into a man — is exactly right for Matthew 13:52.

expand to see more

INSTRUCT, v.t. — To teach; to inform the mind; to educate; to impart knowledge to one who was destitute of it.

To direct; to enjoin; to persuade; to give orders to; as, the minister was instructed to negotiate.

INSTRUCTED, pp. — Taught; informed; educated; directed.

From the Latin instruo, to build in, to furnish, to equip — the root of structure.

Webster’s note on the etymology recovers what English has lost: instruction furnishes a man as a storehouse is furnished.

Key Scripture

Matthew 13:52 — "Then said he unto them, Therefore every scribe which is instructed unto the kingdom of heaven is like unto a man that is an householder, which bringeth forth out of his treasure things new and old."

Acts 18:25 — "This man was instructed in the way of the Lord; and being fervent in the spirit, he spake and taught diligently the things of the Lord, knowing only the baptism of John."

Philippians 4:12 — "I know both how to be abased, and I know how to abound: every where and in all things I am instructed both to be full and to be hungry, both to abound and to suffer need."

Jeremiah 6:8 — "Be thou instructed, O Jerusalem, lest my soul depart from thee; lest I make thee desolate, a land not inhabited."

2 Timothy 3:16 — "All scripture is given by inspiration of God, and is profitable for doctrine, for reproof, for correction, for instruction in righteousness:"

Modern Corruption

Discipleship has been widely reduced to information delivery on one side and to unstructured relationship on the other, and Matthew 13:52 describes something neither of them is: a furnished householder who can bring out the right thing at the right time.

expand to see more

The scribe instructed unto the kingdom brings forth things new and old, which means he has both testaments in his treasure and knows which the hour requires. That is a competence, and it is built into a man over years by teaching, reading, memory, and use. Two modern failures stand on either side of it. One fills the storehouse and never opens it — the man who has attended everything and can apply nothing. The other opens a bare storehouse — the ministry of warm relationship without content, which has nothing to bring out when a real trouble arrives. Paul’s charge to Timothy joins the two: the things that thou hast heard of me among many witnesses, the same commit thou to faithful men, who shall be able to teach others also.

Philippians 4:12 corrects the assumption that instruction happens only in a room. Paul uses the vocabulary of initiation — he has been let into a secret — and the curriculum he names is being full and being hungry, abounding and suffering need. Contentment was learned, and the teacher was providence. This is why the catechism, the sermon, and the shipwreck are not rival schools. A believer who has been taught sound doctrine and never had it tested has been half instructed; a believer who has suffered much and been taught little has been half instructed the other way. Jeremiah’s plea puts the alternative starkly: Be thou instructed, O Jerusalem, lest my soul depart from thee.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Greek matheteuo (G3100), to be made a disciple, at Matthew 13:52; katecheo (G2727), to instruct orally, whence catechism, at Acts 18:25; mueo (G3453), to initiate, at Philippians 4:12.

expand to see more

Greek matheteuo (G3100) — to be discipled, to be instructed as a learner; Matthew 13:52 and 28:19.

Greek katecheo (G2727) — to sound down into the ears, to instruct orally; Acts 18:25, Luke 1:4, Galatians 6:6 — the root of catechism.

Greek mueo (G3453) — to initiate into the mysteries; I am instructed both to be full and to be hungry (Philippians 4:12).

Greek paideia (G3809) — instruction, training, chastening; instruction in righteousness (2 Timothy 3:16).

Hebrew yasar (H3256) — to chasten, to instruct; be thou instructed, O Jerusalem (Jeremiah 6:8), where teaching and discipline are one word.

Usage

"Every scribe which is instructed unto the kingdom of heaven (Matthew 13:52) — a furnished storehouse, new and old."

"Instructed in the way of the Lord… knowing only the baptism of John (Acts 18:25) — real teaching, still incomplete."

"I am instructed both to be full and to be hungry (Philippians 4:12) — contentment as a learned skill."
